newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lamfalussy sees need for stability council - paper.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy sees need for stability council - paper.

text.p: European Monetary Institute head Alexandre Lamfalussy said in a newspaper interview published on Tuesday that he believed there was a need for a stability council to step up co-ordination of economic policies after the launch of the single currency in 1999.
In an interview with French business daily Les Echos he noted that the Maastricht treaty called for co-ordinated policies throughout the European Union.
"But there will be a greater obligation among the members (of the euro) to co-ordinate. We are talking about the policy mix," he said.
He said politicians and the future European Central Bank (ECB) had common interests and shared responsibilities in exchange rate policy.

Politicians could, according to the treaty, draw up broad guidelines on policies for exchange rates against currencies outside the European Union, but this was not allowed to interfere with the Bank's role of maintaining price stability.

"But for these joint responsibilities to work efficiently, we need channels of communication," he said. Because of this the treaty said that the chairman of the finance ministers' council (Ecofin) should attend ECB meetings.

"But there is a practical problem. Can the chairman of the Ecofin represent the interests of the countries in EMU if, giving the rotating presidency of the EU, he is the finance minister of a country which is not a member," he said.
"There, in my eyes, is an additional justification for the stability council," he said.
Lamfalussy also said Europe had made progress in reducing budget deficits and inflation but still needed to tackle structural reform to reduce high unemployment.
"With or without Maastricht, I believe the reduction in unemployment is the major challenge which European governments must tackle," he said.
He also said the European Monetary Institute would be "cautious" in recommending which countries he believed should qualify to join EMU at the start in 1999.
It would look at the "reference values" in the treaty calling for a reduction in budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product and in debt to 60 percent of GDP.
"The third, very important factor, is viability," he said.
"The convergence process must be viable through time. A 'good' budget level which clearly is not going to last more than a year should not be accepted," he said.
Once the countries joining EMU were chosen, those waiting to join must be subjected to exactly the same judgements.
"You cannot say to a country which is not joining -- we will see in two years time.
"You have to say, we will look at this again in a year, and if you have met the criteria in the same way as those which have just joined, you will be admitted," he said.

Lamfalussy also repeated that he believed the European Union should make an announcement on fixing exchange rates among those in the euro zone at the same time as it named the first EMU members in April/May 1998 to head of currency speculation.
Lamfalussy is due to step down next month as EMI head, to be replaced by Dutch central bank head Wim Duisenberg.
